schools.summary: Gill has heard the same sayings from teachers and parents and calls the repetition nauseous rather than merely needless.
Henry warns that the saw of contention grows hotter the longer it is drawn, and separates needless repetition from unskilful application.
Clarke turns the verse into a charge of pretended consolation; Wesley extends the triviality to all creatures before a soul under conviction.
Ellicott reads the speech as an abandonment of argument; Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase as troublesome comforters.
Gregory the Great makes the friends' slander a pattern of how the wicked charge their own faults on the good, and the sufferer's patience a type of the Church.

debates.question: What is the character of this reply?

sides.position: A retort in kind, easy and endless, which stirs passion without convincing judgement
Not argument at all, but complaint, appeal and a declaration that the case is desperate
The forbearance of a holy man who bears what he never did, and so figures the Church

outliers.note: The only patristic voice here, and the only one who reads the quarrel as a type of the Church bearing with those she cannot correct.

themes: I have heard many such things
put your soul in my soul's stead
1.pericope_label: Miserable comforters are ye all; shall vain words have an end?

schools.summary: Gill turns the offer into two questions, whether he ought to speak so and whether he would, and answers both from conscience.
Henry sets out the double bind, that speaking brought no ease and silence brought no nearer anything.
Clarke prefers plain futures with Mr. Good and reports a rendering that makes the promise a threat of unanswerable speech.
Ellicott raises the crux of the head-shaking, which may be mockery or sympathy, and notes the phrase differs from the one used elsewhere for derision.

debates.question: Is the shaking of the head here mockery or sympathy?

sides.position: Mockery, in contrast with the comfort offered in the next verse
Possibly sympathy, in parallel with it, since the phrase is not the one used elsewhere for derision

outliers.note: Alone in reporting Mr. Good's rendering, in which the speaker would overpower his friends with his own mouth until his lips failed.

themes: if your soul were in my soul's stead
4.pericope_label: I also could speak as ye do; but my grief is not eased

schools.summary: Gill traces the weariness to God and reads the wrinkles as affliction's furrows, not age's.
Clarke reports the Latin and Mr. Good, suggests elephantiasis, and refers the tearing to Satan permitted to show himself; Wesley makes every enemy God's archer.
Keil and Delitzsch work the rare verb for wrinkling; Ellicott notes the oscillation between speaking of God and addressing him.

debates.question: Who is the enemy that tears him in wrath?

sides.position: God, though on a mistaken apprehension of one who hates none of his creatures
God, plainly, since he is openly named just afterwards
Satan and his demons, permitted to show themselves, since the figures are too strong for three human friends
The neighbours who envied his prosperity, at least in the mocking verses

outliers.note: Alone in making Satan visible in the scene, and in quoting Mr. Heath's reading of the whole passage as a hunting metaphor.

themes: he teareth me in his wrath
7.pericope_label: He hath made me weary; he teareth me in his wrath

schools.summary: Gill lists four candidates for the wicked one and carries the gaping mouths over to the passion of Christ.
Wesley makes the same typological application and supplies the wrestler and the target for the shaking and the mark.
Keil and Delitzsch work the two intensive verbs of breaking; Ellicott hears a retort in the words ungodly and wicked.

debates.question: Who are the ungodly into whose hands he was delivered?

sides.position: Satan, or Eliphaz, or the friends collectively, or the raiders who took his goods
The friends, on whom he retorts the terms they had used of others

outliers.note: Alone in giving the passage its memorable image, the sufferer become a St. Sebastian for the arrows of God.

10.pericope_label: They have gaped upon me with their mouth; God hath delivered me to the wicked

schools.summary: Gill offers four identifications of the archers and keeps the sackcloth literal and voluntary.
Clarke writes the chapter's longest note, on the horn as an emblem of power still worn on the forehead in Abyssinia; Wesley reads the whole as deliberate self-abasement.
Keil and Delitzsch attribute the sewing of sackcloth to the body's distortion by disease; Ellicott makes the skin itself the comparison.

debates.question: Why was the sackcloth sewed to the skin?

sides.position: Because elephantiasis had so distorted the body that ordinary clothing would not serve
Because the skin itself had grown hard and rugged as sackcloth, the clause being figurative
Because the mourner resolved to keep his humiliation on as long as the affliction lasted

outliers.note: Alone in documenting the horn from a traveller's account of Abyssinian governors, and in rejecting Mr. Good's turban on that evidence.

13.pericope_label: His archers compass me round about; I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin

schools.summary: Gill bounds the denial carefully, to nothing unjustly got rather than to sinlessness.
Henry divides the conscience toward men and toward God, and makes the purity of prayer depend on the justice of the hands.
Clarke makes it a dying assertion; Wesley adds that the fear and service of God had not been cast off.
Keil and Delitzsch prefer redness to kindling in the eyes and reject a prepositional reading of the next clause; Ellicott compares the construction in Isaiah.

debates.question: What does the foulness of the face mean?

sides.position: Redness all over from weeping, from the root that names the Alhambra
A face swollen and red with excessive tears, as the Arabic sense of the word suggests

outliers.note: Alone in observing that all this misery belongs to a man who is no disguised hypocrite with penance to do.

themes: my face is foul with weeping
16.pericope_label: My face is foul with weeping; not for any injustice in mine hands

schools.summary: Gill makes the verse a curse on himself, that any sin deserving the name of blood might stand published rather than hidden.
Clarke sets out both constructions and prefers the call for vengeance; Wesley takes the second half as the other arm of the curse.
Ellicott reads the cry as one that should fill the whole earth, and treats the witness in heaven as the preparation for the book's great confession.

debates.question: What does the appeal to the earth ask for?

sides.position: Vengeance on his destroyers, as Abel's blood cried against Cain
That his own guilt, if any, should be uncovered rather than hidden

outliers.note: Alone in judging that no other book of the Bible shows faith clinging to the all-just God for justification as this one does.

themes: O earth, cover not my blood
let my cry have no place
18.pericope_label: O earth, cover not my blood; my witness is in heaven

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes what was scorned, the arguments and not the diseases, and gives three forms of the plea for a hearing.
Clarke prefers Mr. Good's rendering of the numbered years and argues that the next chapter's first verse belongs here; Wesley reads the journey as the going to the dead.
Ellicott proposes reading the verse as an apostrophe to the scorners, and raises a critical doubt about the narrative's character.

debates.question: How should the numbered years be taken?

sides.position: Years easily counted, or years allotted and determined
Years already come: the man expected death hourly and could not look for a few more

outliers.note: Alone in suggesting that a tormented man sustaining so long an argument may show the narrative to be an ideal rather than a record.

themes: that one might plead for a man
the way whence I shall not return
20.pericope_label: My friends scorn me; mine eye poureth out tears unto God
